title: How Cave Dwellers Work
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss cave dwellers across prehistory and history: why early humans (mostly nomadic Paleolithic hunter-gatherers) used caves only sometimes, the advantages and dangers of caves, Neanderthals and Denisovans possibly sharing a Croatian cave, and cave art such as Chauvet and Lascaux in France, including pigments, torchlight, and theories about its meaning. The episode also covers Anasazi/Pueblo cliff dwellings, Mountain Hebron cave homes in the West Bank, Spanish and Cappadocian cave dwellings, a Ukrainian cave where Jewish families hid during the Holocaust, modern cave homes, and a listener mail correction on speed versus acceleration.

segments.title: Opening banter and cave art documentary
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about the cold weather and bird feeders, then discuss Werner Herzog's Cave of Forgotten Dreams and comparing Chauvet and Lascaux cave art, including flash photography damage to pigments.

segments.title: Cave dwelling in prehistory
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the Paleolithic hominids who left cave remains were nomadic hunter-gatherers who did not permanently live in caves, and that most Paleolithic people used various shelters.

segments.title: Reasons to use caves and their dangers
segments.summary: Caves offered shelter from weather and animals and a steady temperature, but many were inaccessible, flooded, had unstable gravel slopes, misleading exits, and total darkness. Early people also had other shelter methods such as hide-covered structures and earth dwellings.

segments.title: Paleolithic warfare and Neanderthal and Denisovan cave sharing
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the idea that organized war is relatively recent, then the discovery of Denisovans and their DNA in modern humans, and evidence that Neanderthals, modern humans, and Denisovans may have used a Croatian cave at different times.

segments.title: Mobility strategies and cave art techniques
segments.summary: Archaeologists describe circulating and radiating mobility strategies, with some camps in caves. The hosts describe how cave painters used earthen pigments, charcoal, blown pigment, hands, and cave wall contours, and mention scaffolding and stenciling.

segments.title: Subjects and theories of cave art
segments.summary: Most cave art depicts herd animals such as bison and mammoths, with few humans or plants. Theories include adolescent boys' drawings, female hand prints, and hunting or spiritual purposes, and the hosts note these remain speculation.

segments.title: Cave dwelling cultures around the world
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the word troglodyte, the Anasazi and Pueblo cliff dwellings in the US Southwest, Mountain Hebron in the West Bank, Spanish cave homes, and Cappadocia's underground churches and cities in Turkey.

segments.title: Holocaust cave hiding and modern cave homes
segments.summary: The hosts describe a Ukrainian cave where 38 Jewish family members hid for 511 days during the Holocaust, then discuss modern cave homes in Europe and the appeal of cave living as an environmentally friendly option.

segments.title: Listener mail: speed versus acceleration and outro
segments.summary: A listener corrects the earlier solar sail episode, explaining that acceleration rather than speed is what is dangerous, and the hosts mention a roller coaster concept designed around acceleration. The episode closes with contact info and a sponsor message.
